problem:
Meridian Bank, a fictional bank with customers in India and Singapore, wants to offer instant person to person transfers between the two countries using the UPI and PayNow linkage. A customer in India wants to send money to a family member in Singapore using only the recipient's mobile number, and a customer in Singapore wants to send money to India using the recipient's UPI ID. Both expect the experience to feel like a domestic instant payment.

The linkage is live, but it is not a single domestic rail. It connects two domestic fast payment systems through participating institutions, proxy identifiers and a settlement arrangement, and each side has its own limits, validation and compliance checks. The UPI and PayNow linkage has been live since 21 February 2023, and the initial Indian daily limit was Rs 60,000. The bank must explain the operationalised linkage, the proxy identifiers and the participating institution model, and validate the current scope before teaching it as universal.

The risk of getting this wrong is a failed transfer after the sender is debited, a payment sent to the wrong person because a proxy was not verified, or a customer promise that the corridor cannot keep on a given day.
solution:
Model the linkage as two domestic legs joined by an orchestration layer, not as one domestic payment. The Indian leg runs on UPI rails and the Singapore leg runs on PayNow rails, with the originating bank, the participating institutions and the settlement arrangement each owning a defined part. The customer promise is stated per leg: the originating leg is accepted, the cross-border orchestration is confirmed, and the destination leg credit is confirmed, and the payment is only reported complete when the required confirmations have arrived.

Use proxy identifiers as a lookup, never as proof. A UPI ID, a mobile number or a VPA resolves to a registered name, and the bank shows that name to the sender for explicit confirmation before the money moves. That confirmation is the control that prevents a mistyped proxy sending money to the wrong person. Record the proxy used, the resolved name, the confirmation timestamp and the consent evidence with the payment.

Apply limits as they stand for the corridor and the customer. The initial Indian daily limit for the linkage was Rs 60,000, and the bank must validate the current scope, the participating institutions and the applicable daily limits before promising a transfer. The wider UPI limit of INR 5 lakh applies to specified categories from December 2024 and must not be presented as the linkage limit. Validate the amount against the corridor limit, the customer limit and the destination limit, and reject or split only under a documented rule the customer can see.

Run compliance and fraud checks on both the sender and the resolved beneficiary, with a synchronous decision deadline that fits the instant promise. If a leg fails after the sender is debited, hold the payment in an unknown state, establish whether the debit is provisional or final, and return or compensate funds under the defined scheme process, never by blind resubmission.

decision.question: A Meridian Bank customer in India enters a Singapore mobile number as the PayNow proxy and Rs 50,000 as the amount. The proxy resolves to a name the customer does not recognise. What should the bank do before the money moves?

options.label: A
options.detail: Convert the amount to Singapore dollars first and skip the name check to save time.

options.label: B
options.detail: Show the resolved beneficiary name for customer confirmation, run sanctions and fraud checks, confirm the amount is within the applicable daily limit, and only then proceed on explicit confirmation.

options.label: C
options.detail: Ask the customer to guess the correct name and proceed if the guess is close.

options.label: D
options.detail: Send the payment anyway, since the proxy resolved to a registered account.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because proxy resolution must be confirmed by the customer, compliance checks must still run, and limits must be validated before execution. Option D is wrong because a resolved proxy is not proof the customer intended that beneficiary. Option C is wrong because guessing a beneficiary name is not a control. Option A is wrong because conversion does not replace beneficiary verification.

steps.title: Enters the recipient proxy, either a mobile number, UPI ID or VPA, and the amount in the app
Resolves the proxy to the registered beneficiary name through the linkage directory
Confirms the resolved beneficiary name and the full disclosure of amount, fees and rate
Validates corridor and customer limits and runs sanctions, AML and fraud checks
Debits the sender and initiates the originating domestic leg
Converts and settles through the linkage settlement arrangement
Credits the beneficiary through the destination fast payment system
Confirms the destination credit to the sender with the reference and value date

happy: The sender enters a mobile number proxy, the linkage resolves it to the expected beneficiary name, the sender confirms the name and the disclosed amounts, limit and compliance checks pass, the UPI leg debits the sender, the orchestration settles the transfer, the PayNow leg credits the beneficiary, and the sender receives a confirmed completion with the reference.

negative.title: Proxy resolves to an unexpected name
negative.detail: The sender does not recognise the resolved beneficiary name. Stop the payment before any debit, let the sender correct the proxy, and log the abandoned attempt without creating a payment.

negative.title: Destination leg timeout
negative.detail: The originating leg is accepted but no destination confirmation arrives. Hold the payment in an unknown state, run a status enquiry by reference, never resubmit blindly, and escalate to investigation at the defined timeout.

negative.title: Sender debited but destination fails
negative.detail: The destination system reports a technical failure after the sender debit. Establish whether the debit is provisional or final, return or compensate funds under the defined process, and ensure exactly one financial effect.

negative.title: Amount above the corridor limit
negative.detail: The amount exceeds the applicable daily limit for the linkage. Reject the instruction with a clear explanation of the limit, or offer a documented alternative the customer can accept, and never split the payment silently to evade the limit.

technical: Store the proxy type and value, the resolved beneficiary name, the confirmation timestamp and the consent evidence as structured data linked by a correlation ID across both legs. Model each leg with its own state machine and an overall orchestration state, with timestamps for leg acceptance, settlement and destination confirmation. Make all status handling idempotent so duplicate callbacks cannot double credit or double refund. Validate amounts, currencies and proxy formats at capture, and record the limit source and version used for the decision. Keep the original sender instruction immutable and link every leg event, fee and FX conversion to it for audit and reconciliation.

accounting: Debit the sender account for the agreed amount and fees, credit the linkage settlement account, and post the destination leg on confirmation, with FX conversion posted as a separate entry so the principal, the rate and the fee are each reconcilable. A failed destination leg after debit moves the funds to a suspense account and onto an investigation worklist with an ageing service level, and any return to the sender is posted as a linked reversal, never by editing the original debit. Operations reconcile originating leg debits, settlement account movements and destination confirmations daily, and report proxy mismatch rates and timeout rates as corridor quality measures.
